metadata.title: Pressure Point
metadata.description: You awaken in a damaged deep-sea research module at 3000 meters depth. The hull groans under 300 atmospheres. Dr. Yuki Tanaka — the station's marine biologist — has sealed the module and is deliberately flooding compartments. She calls you 'Subject 7.' Find a way to the surface before the ocean claims you.
metadata.author: ai-generated

setting.ambient_text: The hull moans like a living thing. Water beads on every surface. Beyond the viewport, something luminous drifts in the black.

items.name: Zip Tie Fragment
items.description: A snapped zip tie. The edge is sharp enough to score plastic.

then.text: Industrial-grade zip tie, snapped at the ratchet. The broken end is sharp like a tiny saw blade.

items.name: Dive Multi-Tool
items.description: A compact diving multi-tool with pliers, wire cutters, and a flathead driver.

then.text: Titanium multi-tool rated to 500 ATM. Pliers, wire cutter, flathead, and a small pry bar. Standard deep-sea kit.
You unfold each tool in turn. Everything works. This is the most useful thing you've found.

items.name: UV Penlight
items.description: A small ultraviolet flashlight. Used for detecting fluorescent markers in specimens.

then.text: Compact UV-A penlight. Marine biologists use these to detect fluorescent proteins in deep-sea specimens. The battery indicator shows half charge.
You click it on. A dim violet glow. You notice faint markings on your own wrist — numbers written in fluorescent ink: '7'. Your subject number.

items.name: Crew Log Page
items.description: A torn page from the station log. Water-stained but legible.

then.text: Day 187. Tanaka won't let anyone near Module C. Says the specimens need 'controlled conditions.' Rodriguez tried to radio topside — Tanaka cut the main antenna cable. Emergency frequency is 121.5 MHz but the backup antenna only works on... the rest is torn.
The page describes Tanaka's descent into obsession. The bottom is torn — the frequency info is missing.
Under UV light, someone wrote in fluorescent ink: 'BACKUP FREQ 156.8 MHz — Rodriguez'. Smart thinking, hiding the information from Tanaka.
The UV light reveals hidden writing in fluorescent ink: 'BACKUP FREQ 156.8 MHz — Rodriguez'. Someone anticipated Tanaka's sabotage.

items.name: Hull Sealant Tube
items.description: Emergency polyurethane hull sealant. Rated for extreme pressure.

then.text: DeepSeal Pro — emergency hull patch compound. Apply to crack, hardens in 30 seconds. Rated to 400 ATM. About one-third left in the tube.

items.name: Spare Circuit Board
items.description: A replacement communications circuit board, still in its anti-static sleeve.

then.text: Replacement board for the RCS-4000 radio system. Model matches the damaged board in the console. This could restore communications.

items.name: Coaxial Cable Segment
items.description: A 2-meter length of marine-grade coaxial cable.

then.text: Standard marine coaxial cable, both ends clean-cut. Could replace a damaged section if you had a way to strip and connect the ends.

items.name: Bioluminescent Sample
items.description: A vial of glowing deep-sea organism fluid. It pulses faintly blue-green.

then.text: A sealed vial of bioluminescent fluid from Tanaka's specimens. It pulses rhythmically, like a heartbeat. The creatures outside the viewport seem to respond to it.
You shake the vial. The glow intensifies to brilliant blue-green. Through the viewport, dark shapes shift in response. These things communicate through light.

items.name: Pressure Wrench
items.description: A heavy-duty wrench calibrated for high-pressure fittings.

then.text: A torque-calibrated wrench for deep-sea pressure fittings. The markings go up to 600 ATM. Hefty — could double as a weapon in a pinch.

items.name: Replacement Visor
items.description: A polycarbonate visor rated for deep-sea pressure.

then.text: Crystal-clear polycarbonate rated to 500 ATM. Standard replacement for deep-sea dive helmets. The seal gasket is intact.

items.name: Valve Key
items.description: A square-socket key for operating pipe shut-off valves.

then.text: Standard valve key. Fits the square sockets on the overhead pipe shut-off valves. Yellow handle — matches the ceiling pipe markings.

items.name: Underwater Emergency Flare
items.description: A chemical flare rated for underwater use. Burns magnesium-bright even at depth.

then.text: Magnesium-based underwater flare. Pull-ignition. Burns for 60 seconds at extreme brightness. Would attract every creature within half a kilometer. The label warns: 'INTENSE LIGHT — DO NOT USE NEAR PHOTOSENSITIVE FAUNA.'

items.name: Repaired Antenna Cable
items.description: A coaxial cable segment spliced with the multi-tool. Should carry a signal.

then.text: Your spliced cable. Not pretty, but the connections are solid. Should carry a radio signal to the backup antenna.

items.name: Creature Lure
items.description: A flare wrapped with bioluminescent specimen fluid. Pulsing with eerie light.

then.text: The specimen fluid coating the flare casing pulses in time with the flare's heat. When lit, this should be irresistible to Tanaka's deep-sea creatures. She'd abandon anything to protect her specimens from harm.

combinations.message: You strip both ends of the cable with the multi-tool's wire cutters and prep the connectors. A clean splice — it should carry a signal.
You smear the bioluminescent fluid across the flare casing. It pulses with an alien rhythm. When lit, this will drive Tanaka's precious specimens into a frenzy — and her with them.
You apply sealant around the visor gasket for a pressure-tight seal. It'll hold for one ascent.

objects.name: Bulkhead Door
objects.description: A heavy steel bulkhead with a wheel-lock mechanism. The status light is red.

then.text: A pressure bulkhead rated for 500 ATM. The status light glows red — sealed from the other side. Through the reinforced glass porthole, you see Dr. Tanaka's lab. She moves between tanks of luminous creatures, humming to herself.
You jammed the bulkhead wheel with the pressure wrench. It won't spin — Tanaka is locked out. But you can hear her pounding from the other side.
You strain against the wheel lock. It's electronically sealed — brute force won't open it.

messages: "Dr. Tanaka! Let me out!" Through the porthole, she pauses, then smiles. "Subject 7 is awake. Wonderful. Your adaptation data will be invaluable."
"Please! I'm not your experiment!" She doesn't even look up. "All subjects express initial reluctance. It passes. Usually."
"Why are you doing this?!" She presses her face to the glass. "Because they SPOKE to me, Subject 7. The deep ones. They need us to understand pressure. Real pressure."

then.text: You wedge the wrench into the wheel mechanism. It locks the wheel solid — even if Tanaka unseals the door electronically, she can't spin the wheel to open it. You've locked HER out.

You crack the flare and press the pulsing lure against the porthole glass. The bioluminescent fluid blazes. Through the glass, Tanaka's specimens go berserk in their tanks. She screams: "NO! My children! What are you DOING?!" She abandons everything to tend to them.

objects.name: Observation Viewport
objects.description: A thick acrylic viewport looking into the abyss.

then.text: Absolute blackness — then movement. Bioluminescent shapes drift past: jellyfish trailing curtains of blue light, angular fish with glowing lures. Beautiful and alien. The pressure out there would crush you to nothing.

More creatures now, drawn by the station's lights. They cluster against the glass, pulsing in coordinated patterns. Are they... communicating? One massive tentacle slides across the viewport, slow and deliberate.
The creatures are pressed against every viewport now. Hundreds of them. Pulsing in unison. The glass creaks. They're not just watching anymore — they're pushing.
You press your hand against the acrylic. It's frigid. Three inches of polycarbonate between you and 300 atmospheres of pressure. Don't think about it.
"Is anyone out there?" Stupid question. Nothing out there but crushing darkness, freezing water, and things that glow. None of them can help you.

objects.name: Specimen Holding Tanks
objects.description: Three sealed cylindrical tanks. Things move inside them.

then.text: Three pressurized tanks filled with murky seawater. Bioluminescent organisms drift inside — some recognizable (jellyfish, cephalopods), others... not. One tank is labeled 'SUBJECT PREPARATION — DO NOT OPEN.' The fluid inside is a sickly yellow-green.
The organisms pulse in synchrony. The 'Subject Preparation' tank bubbles ominously.
The tank valves are locked. You could force one open, but pressurized seawater at this depth would spray everywhere — and whatever's inside would come with it.

You could crack a tank valve with this, but releasing pressurized specimens would flood the immediate area and attract Tanaka's attention instantly. That might be exactly what you want — or a fatal mistake.
You find a sampling port on the side of the nearest tank. You twist it open carefully and collect a vial of glowing fluid. The organisms inside the tank swirl aggressively toward the port.

objects.name: Laboratory Bench
objects.description: A stainless steel bench covered in research equipment and notes.

then.text: A disaster of research notes, specimen slides, and equipment. A UV penlight sits among the debris. Tanaka's handwriting covers the margins of every page: 'They respond to pressure changes. They COMMUNICATE. Subject 7 will prove it.'
You've already picked through the debris. Research notes about bioluminescent communication, pressure adaptation studies, and increasingly unhinged margin notes.
You rifle through the papers. Most are incomprehensible research data. But between the pages, you find a torn crew log page and spot the UV penlight.

objects.name: Dive Equipment Locker
objects.description: A tall metal locker with 'EMERGENCY EVA' stenciled on it.

then.text: A reinforced locker for emergency dive equipment. Padlocked. Through the ventilation slits, you can see a dive suit, tanks, and gear inside. You could hide inside if you got it open — it's big enough.
Inside: a partial dive suit, helmet mounts, and a rack of equipment. The dive closeup panel gives you access to everything in detail.
The padlock holds firm. Standard marine padlock — you'd need a tool.
You work the multi-tool's pry bar against the padlock hasp. It pops free with a metallic snap. The locker swings open, revealing a treasure trove of dive equipment.
The zip tie fragment is sharp but too flimsy to defeat the padlock. You need something with more leverage.

objects.name: Deck Grate
objects.description: A heavy metal grate set into the floor. Water pools beneath it.

then.text: A steel floor grate over the bilge channel. Water sloshes beneath it — more than there should be. Four bolts hold it down. Something glints in the water below.
The bilge channel runs beneath the floor. Ankle-deep water flows toward the pump station. Too narrow to crawl through, but useful for moving small objects between compartments.
The bolts are tight. You'd need a tool to remove them.
You work the bolts loose one by one with the flathead driver. The last bolt pops free and the grate lifts. Below: ankle-deep seawater and — there — a valve key wedged against the pipe junction.

objects.name: Emergency Systems Panel
objects.description: A red-bordered panel with 'EMERGENCY SYSTEMS' stenciled above it.

then.text: Emergency systems panel. Behind the locked cover: ascent pod controls, emergency beacon, backup power switch. A keypad lock requires a 4-digit code. The label reads: 'CODE ON STATION REGISTRY — CAPTAIN'S COPY.'
The panel is open. Inside: the emergency beacon switch, backup power bus, and the ascent pod release controls. The pressure control station is accessible from here too.
The cover won't budge. Electronic keypad lock — you need the code.
The panel is designed to resist forced entry — it's an emergency system, not a snack cabinet. You need the code.

objects.name: Overhead Pipe Network
objects.description: A maze of pipes running along the ceiling. Some are sweating, some are hissing.

then.text: A network of pipes — water, air, ballast, communications conduit. Several are sweating condensation. One pipe has a hairline crack, dripping steadily. Yellow-marked shut-off valves require a square-socket key. The ballast lines run to the pressure control station.
The cracked pipe is sealed with hull sealant. The dripping has stopped, but the other pipes still groan under pressure.
You've shut off the flood valves and redirected pressure to the ballast system. The pipes thrum with redirected force — all that energy is now feeding the ballast tanks.
You press your thumb over the crack. Water sprays between your fingers — the pressure is incredible. You can't hold it.
You apply the DeepSeal compound to the crack. It foams, hardens, and holds. The dripping stops. One less way for the ocean to get in.

You insert the valve key into the ballast redirect junction. One full turn. The pipes shudder, then roar with redirected pressure. All flood water pressure is now feeding the emergency ballast blow system.
You could redirect the pipe pressure, but the flood valves are still open — the system would just push more water in. Close the flood valves at the pressure control station first.
You need to seal the crack first or any pressure redirect will just spray seawater everywhere.

objects.name: Supply Crate
objects.description: A large plastic supply crate, partially crushed.

then.text: A large supply crate, lid cracked from pressure damage. You could squeeze inside to hide. Stenciled on the side: 'STATION SUPPLY — MODULE B — REG# 0451.'
0451... that number seems like it could be important.
Inside the crate: dive supplies, ration packs, and hull sealant tubes. You've already taken what's useful.

You pry the cracked lid open. Inside: emergency ration packs (expired), a hull sealant tube, and a coaxial cable segment wrapped in plastic. The registration number is stamped inside the lid too: '0451.'

objects.name: Dive Suit Rack
objects.description: A wall-mounted rack where dive equipment hangs.

then.text: Empty mounting brackets. The suits are stored in the dive locker. But you notice a multi-tool hanging from a lanyard on one hook — someone's personal kit, left behind in the evacuation.
You grab the multi-tool and clip it to your belt. Titanium and perfectly maintained. This changes things.
You already have the multi-tool. Nothing else here.

objects.name: Intercom Speaker
objects.description: A wall-mounted intercom. The light blinks intermittently.

then.text: The intercom crackles with static. Tanaka uses this to monitor — and taunt — her 'subjects.' The speaker is wired into the station's internal communication system.

messages: You press the talk button. Tanaka's voice comes back immediately: "Subject 7, please conserve your oxygen. Hyperventilation reduces data quality."
"Let me go!" Static. Then: "Pressure adaptation is not voluntary, Subject 7. Ask the anglerfish. Ask the tube worms. They didn't choose the deep either."
"You're insane!" A long pause. Then, almost sadly: "They all say that. Until they hear the singing. The deep ones sing, Subject 7. You'll hear it soon."

then.text: You could rip it off the wall, but it's hardwired — Tanaka can listen through the other intercoms anyway. Better to not draw attention.

objects.name: Spreading Puddle
objects.description: Seawater pooling on the deck, growing slowly.

then.text: A thin film of seawater spreading across the deck. It seeps from somewhere below — the bilge pumps should handle this, but they're barely running. Faint bioluminescent specks glow in the water. Even the puddles carry life at this depth.
The water is ankle-deep now and rising. You can feel the cold through your shoes. The bioluminescent organisms have multiplied — the floor glows with ghostly blue light.
Knee-deep. Freezing. The water is thick with bioluminescent organisms — the whole floor pulses with alien light. Every step sends ripples of blue-green. This module is sinking.
Ice cold. Your fingers go numb in seconds. The water tastes of salt and something metallic — hull corrosion.

objects.name: Ventilation Shaft Cover
objects.description: A rectangular vent cover near the ceiling.

then.text: A ventilation shaft cover, four screws holding it in place. Cold air hisses through the slats. You can hear the station's life support system humming beyond.
The vent shaft opening. Too narrow to crawl through, but you can see into the next module — Tanaka's main lab. She's pacing between tanks, muttering to her specimens.
The screws are recessed — you can't grip them with your fingers.
Four screws, four turns each. The cover swings open. Through the shaft, you can see into Tanaka's module — and more importantly, she can hear you. Sound carries perfectly through the ductwork.

You crack the flare and toss it into the shaft. Blinding light fills the ductwork. From the other side, Tanaka screams — the flare's light is agitating every specimen in her lab. "MY CHILDREN! Subject 7, WHAT HAVE YOU DONE?!" She scrambles to cover the tanks.

You whisper into the shaft. Tanaka's voice drifts back, distorted by the ductwork: "I can hear you breathing, Subject 7. The deep ones hear it too. They're drawn to carbon dioxide, you know. Like sharks to blood."

objects.name: Deep-Sea Dive Helmet
objects.description: A professional deep-sea diving helmet. The visor is cracked.

then.text: A deep-sea dive helmet with a cracked polycarbonate visor. At surface pressure it would be fine, but at 3000 meters? That crack would catastrophically fail. You'd need a replacement visor and sealant to make it pressure-worthy.
The replacement visor is sealed in place. Not factory-quality, but it should hold for one ascent. Combined with an air supply and the ascent pod, this could save your life.
You pick it up. Heavier than expected. The cracked visor spider-webs under your touch — it's barely holding together.
You pop the cracked visor out and seat the replacement. Without sealant, it's just sitting there — the pressure would blow it off instantly.
Sealant alone won't fix it — you need a replacement visor first. Sealing over a cracked polycarbonate is a death sentence at pressure.

objects.name: Air Tank Rack
objects.description: A rack of high-pressure breathing tanks. Most gauges read empty.

then.text: Eight tank slots, seven showing red (empty). One tank in the back shows amber — partial fill, maybe 15 minutes of breathing time. Better than nothing for an emergency ascent.
All tanks empty or removed. You have the partial tank.
You pull the amber-gauge tank free. Behind it, wedged in the rack: an emergency underwater flare. You grab that too.
You pull the amber-gauge tank free. About 15 minutes of air. Every breath counts.

objects.name: Local Pressure Gauge
objects.description: An analog pressure gauge mounted on the dive station bulkhead.

then.text: Module internal pressure: 1.2 ATM. Slightly above normal — the hull is weeping. External: 295 ATM. The needle trembles.
Internal pressure: 2.1 ATM and climbing. Water is compressing the air. External still 295 ATM. The differential is shrinking — that's not good.
Internal: 4.8 ATM. The gauge needle is in the red zone. At this rate, the module will lose structural integrity in minutes.

objects.name: Maintenance Toolbox
objects.description: A mounted toolbox with a latch.

then.text: A wall-mounted maintenance toolbox. The latch is stiff but not locked.
You wrestle the latch open. Inside: a pressure wrench and a replacement dive helmet visor in a padded case. Both could be critical.
Empty except for some cable ties and rust.
Digging deeper into the toolbox, beneath the rust and old cable ties, you find a spare circuit board in an anti-static bag. Standard marine radio replacement board — exactly what the console needs.

objects.name: Suit Repair Kit
objects.description: A small kit for patching dive suit seals.

then.text: A dive suit seal repair kit. Patches, adhesive, and pressure-test strips. If the dive suit in the locker has seal damage, this could fix it.
You check the kit contents. Complete — patches for every standard seal point. You'll need the suit itself to work on.

objects.name: Emergency Beacon
objects.description: A handheld EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon).

then.text: A deep-sea emergency beacon. At this depth, the signal can't reach the surface directly — but if triggered inside the ascent pod during ascent, it would broadcast your position the moment you hit comms depth around 200 meters.
The beacon blinks red. It's broadcasting — but at 3000m, the signal goes nowhere. You need to ascend first.
You flip the activation switch. The beacon starts pulsing red. At this depth the signal is useless, but during an ascent it would be your lifeline.

objects.name: Depth Reference Chart
objects.description: A wall chart showing station depth, pressure ratings, and emergency ascent profiles.

then.text: Station ABYSSAL-7 depth profile. Current depth: 3,012m. Emergency ascent pod rated to 3,500m. Ascent time to surface: 8 minutes (emergency blow). Required: sealed helmet, air supply (15 min minimum), pressurized pod. Note: 'Pod release requires BOTH manual lever AND electronic override. Code matches station registry number.'
Depth: 3,012m. Ascent pod needs: sealed helmet, air supply, manual lever AND electronic override (code = station registry). Eight minutes to the surface.

objects.name: Radio Console
objects.description: The station's communications console. Most indicators are dark.

then.text: The RCS-4000 communications console. The main circuit board has been pulled out and smashed — Tanaka's work. An empty board slot gapes like a missing tooth. The antenna cable junction shows a clean cut — also sabotaged. But the rest of the hardware looks intact. If you could replace the circuit board and splice the antenna cable...

The replacement board is seated and the antenna cable is spliced. The console hums with power. The frequency dial reads 121.5 MHz — standard emergency. But the crew log mentioned a backup frequency...
The console is broadcasting your mayday on 156.8 MHz. The signal strength meter bounces — it's getting through. Now you just need to survive until rescue arrives... or find a faster way out.
You examine the damage. The circuit board is destroyed beyond repair — you need a replacement. The antenna cable is cleanly cut — it could be spliced with a new segment and the right tools.
You seat the replacement board and connect the spliced antenna cable. The console powers up — lights flicker across the panel, then stabilize. The communications system is operational.
The board slots in perfectly, but without an antenna cable, there's no signal path. You need to repair the severed antenna connection too.
You splice the cable into the junction. Good connection. But without a functioning circuit board, the radio is still dead.

objects.name: Frequency Dial
objects.description: A large tuning dial for the radio system.

then.text: The frequency tuning dial. Currently set to 121.5 MHz — the universal emergency frequency. But Tanaka probably monitors that. The crew log hinted at a backup frequency...
Turning the dial accomplishes nothing with a dead radio.
You could broadcast on 121.5 MHz — the emergency frequency — but Tanaka might be monitoring it. You need the backup frequency. The crew log mentioned it, but the information was incomplete...

objects.name: Radio Handset
objects.description: A corded radio handset hanging from its cradle.

then.text: Standard radio handset. Push-to-talk button on the side.

You key the handset: "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY. This is Station ABYSSAL-7, depth 3000 meters. Crew member held captive by Dr. Tanaka. Module flooding. Request immediate rescue. Position on beacon frequency." Static... then: "ABYSSAL-7, this is research vessel DEPTH STAR. We read you. Rescue submersible deploying. ETA forty minutes. Hold on." Forty minutes. You might not have forty minutes.

You pick up the handset. Broadcasting on 121.5 might reach the surface — but Tanaka monitors the emergency frequency. She'd know you've repaired the radio and escalate immediately. Find the backup frequency first.
Dead air. The radio isn't operational.

"ABYSSAL-7 to DEPTH STAR — still here. Module flooding, situation critical." The reply crackles: "Copy, ABYSSAL-7. Rescue ETA thirty-five minutes. Can you reach the ascent pod?" You could — if you can solve the pod release.

objects.name: Station Logbook
objects.description: The official station logbook, water-stained and worn.

then.text: Station ABYSSAL-7 Operations Log. The last entry is from the captain: 'Day 193. Tanaka has barricaded Module C. Rodriguez and Chen are missing. I've hidden the backup radio frequency where she can't find it — not without the right light. Emergency code remains station standard. If anyone reads this: GET OUT. — Capt. Vasquez.'
You sweep the UV light across the pages. On the inside back cover, glowing violet text appears: 'BACKUP FREQ 156.8 MHz — Rodriguez.' And below, in the captain's writing: 'God help us all.'
The hidden text still glows under UV: backup frequency 156.8 MHz.

objects.name: Smashed Circuit Board
objects.description: The radio's main circuit board, destroyed beyond repair.

then.text: The radio's circuit board, smashed to fragments. Tanaka was thorough — every IC is cracked. You'll need a replacement board entirely.
Fragments of green PCB and bent pins. Beyond repair. You need a spare.

objects.name: Antenna Cable Junction
objects.description: Where the antenna cable meets the radio — cut clean through.

then.text: The antenna coaxial cable has been cut with surgical precision. About 20cm of cable is missing — Tanaka removed a whole segment. You'd need a replacement cable segment and tools to splice it.
Your spliced cable connects the antenna to the radio. The connection holds.

objects.name: Sonar Display
objects.description: A circular sonar display, still operational.

then.text: The sonar shows the station surrounded by small contacts — the bioluminescent creatures. They circle the station in lazy patterns. One large contact sits motionless on the seabed nearby.
The creature contacts have multiplied. They're closing in. The large seabed contact has moved — it's directly beneath the station now. Something very big is down there.
The sonar is overwhelmed — hundreds of contacts, all converging on the station. The large contact is directly below, and it's... rising.

You hit the active ping button. PING. The sonar sweeps outward. Every creature contact freezes for a moment — then they scatter. In about 30 seconds they'll regroup, but the ping carries through the hull. Tanaka heard it.

objects.name: Master Pressure Gauge
objects.description: The main pressure monitoring system for the station.

then.text: Hull integrity: 87%. Internal pressure climbing slowly. The gauge shows all three ballast tanks: empty, partially filled, and full. The emergency blow system needs all three tanks full of compressed air to surface the module.

Hull integrity: 71%. Two hull sections amber, one red. If the ballast tanks could be filled and the emergency blow activated, the module would rocket to the surface — but the flood valves are feeding water in, not air.
Hull integrity: 52% and dropping. Multiple sections critical. Either surface this module NOW or get to the ascent pod. There's no more time.

objects.name: Ballast Control Panel
objects.description: Controls for the station's ballast tank system.

then.text: The ballast control system. Three toggle switches control compressed air routing to the ballast tanks. Currently locked by the safety interlock — you need to close the flood valves first, then redirect pipe pressure, then blow the tanks. It's a multi-step system designed to prevent accidental surfacing.
The safety interlock is green — flood valves closed, pipe pressure redirected. The ballast tank toggles are armed. Set the correct pattern and hit the emergency blow.
The controls are interlocked. The display reads: 'BALLAST BLOW SEQUENCE: 1. Close flood valves. 2. Redirect pipe pressure. 3. Set fill pattern. 4. Execute blow.' Steps 1 and 2 aren't complete.
With flood valves closed and pressure redirected, the safety interlock clicks green. The ballast toggle switches are now armed. Set the correct fill pattern to prepare the emergency blow.

objects.name: Ascent Pod Release Lever
objects.description: A heavy red lever labeled 'EMERGENCY ASCENT — PULL TO RELEASE.'

then.text: The manual release lever for the emergency ascent pod. A sign reads: 'DUAL AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED — Manual lever AND electronic override must both be activated. Pod accommodates 1 person. Ensure pressure suit is sealed before release.'

You seal the dive helmet, check your air supply, and pull the lever. CLANK. The pod hatch opens with a hiss of pressurized air. You climb in, seal it behind you, and slam the ascent button. Explosive bolts fire. The pod rockets upward through 3000 meters of black water. The pressure eases. Light appears above. You break the surface in a geyser of foam. The emergency beacon screams your position. You're alive.

then.reason: You launched the emergency ascent pod and rocketed to the surface. Dr. Tanaka and her abyssal horrors shrink to nothing below. Rescue vessels home in on your beacon.

then.text: The pod is unlocked, but you have no air supply. Eight minutes in a sealed pod with no breathing gas would kill you long before you reached the surface.
The pod is unlocked, but your dive helmet has a cracked visor. During ascent, the pressure differential would shatter it. You need to fix the visor first.
The lever won't budge. The electronic override hasn't been activated — dual authorization required. You need to enter the release code on the override panel.

objects.name: Flood Valve Array
objects.description: A row of motorized valves controlling water intake to the module.

then.text: Four motorized flood valves — all open, feeding seawater into the module. Tanaka opened them remotely. The electronic controls are locked, but each valve has a manual override wheel. You'd need a valve key to turn them.
All four flood valves are shut. The water is no longer rising — but what's already in the module isn't going anywhere either.
The valve wheels are square-socket — they need a specific key. You can't grip them with bare hands.

You fit the valve key and crank each valve shut. One... two... three... four. The roar of incoming water dies to silence. The module groans — the pressure is still there, but no more water is coming in.

objects.name: Hull Integrity Display
objects.description: A digital display showing structural integrity across all module sections.

then.text: Hull integrity display. Module B (you're here): 87%. Module A (Tanaka's lab): 95%. Module C: OFFLINE. External hull: minor stress fractures in sections 4 and 7. The station was built for permanent depth — but not for deliberate flooding.
Module B: 71% and dropping. Module A: 92%. Module C: OFFLINE. Sections 4 and 7 now critical. The display flashes red warnings.
Module B: 52%. STRUCTURAL FAILURE IMMINENT. The display is screaming. Every section is red or amber. You can hear the hull flexing — the metal is singing.

objects.name: Electronic Override Panel
objects.description: A keypad panel for entering the emergency system override code.

then.text: Electronic override keypad. A 4-digit code unlocks the emergency ascent pod release. The label says the code matches the station registry number.
The override panel shows green — code accepted. The ascent pod electronic lock is released. Now you need the manual lever too.
The keypad awaits a 4-digit code. The station registry number...

objects.name: Zip Tie Restraints
objects.description: Heavy-duty zip ties binding your wrists to the chair armrest. Industrial grade, but the plastic is cold and brittle.

states.bound: The zip ties dig into your wrists. Thick plastic, industrial grade.
states.broken: Shattered plastic fragments litter the floor. You're free.

then.text: Heavy-duty zip ties, the kind used for industrial cable bundling. Your wrists are bound to the chair's metal armrest. But the cold has made the plastic brittle — you can feel it cracking when you flex.
You flex your wrists hard against the cold plastic. SNAP. The brittle zip ties shatter. You're free. A sharp fragment of plastic falls to the floor — could be useful as a makeshift shiv.
Broken plastic fragments on the floor. You're free to move.

on_solve.text: BEEP. The panel clicks open, revealing the emergency systems: ascent pod controls, backup power, and pressure control station access.

on_fail.text: BZZT. Wrong code. The keypad flashes red.

on_max_fail.text: The keypad locks out after too many wrong attempts. A backup mechanical release catches your eye — the multi-tool might work on the panel screws.

on_solve.text: The correct pattern! Compressed air roars into the ballast tanks. The entire station shudders, then LURCHES upward. Alarms scream. Through the viewport, the ocean floor drops away. You're ascending — the whole module, rocketing toward the surface.

effects.text: The ascent takes eight agonizing minutes. The hull screams. Creatures scatter. Light grows above. Then — BREACH. The module erupts through the surface in a fountain of spray. Sunlight. Wind. Air. You're alive. The entire station module bobs on the waves, its emergency beacon wailing.

effects.reason: You blew the ballast tanks and surfaced the entire research module. Dr. Tanaka, trapped in Module A, surfaces with you — screaming about her ruined specimens. Rescue ships are already converging on your beacon signal.

on_fail.text: Wrong pattern. The tanks pressurize unevenly — the module lurches sideways before the safety system resets. Try again.

on_solve.text: The dial clicks to 156.8 MHz — Rodriguez's backup frequency. The signal meter jumps. This frequency bypasses Tanaka's monitoring. You're clear to transmit.

messages: You pick up deep-sea hydrophone noise. Clicks and groans from the abyss. Not helpful.
Faint signal — but it's one of Tanaka's specimen monitoring frequencies. Don't linger here.

phases.name: Seepage

on_enter.text: Your head pounds. The air is cold and tastes of salt. You're zip-tied to a chair in what looks like a research lab module. Water beads on the walls and pools on the deck. Beyond the viewport, the abyss stares back.

phases.ambient_text: Steady dripping. The hull creaks rhythmically. Something bioluminescent drifts past the viewport.

phases.name: Flooding

on_enter.text: A deep GROAN shakes the module. A pipe in the ceiling splits and seawater sprays across the deck. The water level is rising visibly now. Tanaka's voice crackles over the intercom: "Phase two, Subject 7. The pressure is increasing. Your body will adapt... or it won't."

phases.ambient_text: Water sloshing. Hull groaning. Distant metallic clangs as the station flexes under pressure.

phases.name: Critical Pressure

on_enter.text: CATASTROPHIC WARNING. The hull is failing. Rivets pop like gunshots. The water is waist-deep and freezing. Every surface is slick. The creatures outside are pressed against every viewport, pulsing in unison, and something MASSIVE moves in the deep below. Tanaka's voice is barely audible over the chaos: "Beautiful... they're calling to the Mother. You'll be part of something magnificent, Subject 7."

phases.ambient_text: Alarms. Rushing water. The hull singing under pressure. Something enormous moving outside.

effects.text: The lights flicker. A deep metallic groan runs through the hull — the station adjusting to increasing internal pressure. A rivet pops somewhere above with a sharp PING.

Something SLAMS against the viewport. You spin — a massive eye, easily a meter across, stares in at you. Bioluminescent patterns ripple across the creature's skin. Then it's gone, sliding back into the dark. The creatures know you're here.

The intercom crackles: "Subject 7, your cortisol levels must be fascinating right now. I wish I could take a sample. Don't worry — the pressure adaptation process is survivable. Mostly. The last three subjects... well. You're different. I can feel it."

A THUNDEROUS crash from below. The floor buckles. An alarm screams: 'MODULE C — HULL BREACH. MODULE C — CATASTROPHIC FAILURE.' Module C — the one that was offline — just imploded. The station lurches. If Module B goes next...

Every creature outside begins pulsing in synchrony. Blue. Green. Blue. Green. The rhythm matches your heartbeat. Through the viewport, the deep lights up — not scattered individual creatures, but a single coordinated display stretching into the void. Tanaka's voice, awestruck: "They're singing for you, Subject 7. The Mother is coming. Can you hear Her?"

Tanaka spots the repaired radio through the ventilation shaft. "You FIXED the communications?! Clever, Subject 7. Very clever. But who will come? This depth... by the time they arrive..." Her voice drops to a whisper. "The Mother will be here first."

The hull is screaming. Bolts shearing. Water jets through new cracks. Through the chaos, Tanaka's voice: "She's here. The Mother. Can't you feel her? The pressure... the beautiful pressure... it's almost time, Subject 7." Below the station, something impossibly large PUSHES against the foundations.

killer.name: Dr. Yuki Tanaka
killer.description: Marine biologist. Spent 193 days at depth studying bioluminescent deep-sea organisms. Something she discovered drove her to madness — she believes the creatures are sentient, that they communicate through pressure changes, and that they need human 'subjects' to study in return. Clinical, detached, alternating between cold scientific analysis and manic reverence for 'the deep ones.'

on_approach: Time to check your vitals, Subject 7...
Hold still. I need to observe your stress response.
The deep ones are curious about you. Let me take a closer look.
Routine observation. Don't be alarmed — elevated cortisol is expected.
on_search: Subject 7, hiding skews the data. Please cooperate.
I can hear your breathing. Carbon dioxide output increases 400% under stress — fascinating.
The specimens can sense your heartbeat through the water. There's nowhere to hide from them.
Come now. The Mother doesn't like it when her subjects resist.
on_clear: Hmm. Resting heart rate acceptable. Carry on.
Subject 7 appears stable. Resuming specimen monitoring.
Good. Stay calm. The adaptation process works better when you're relaxed.
on_evidence: Someone's been busy. Adaptation-driven problem-solving — I'll note that in your file.
You've been tampering with equipment, Subject 7. The deep ones won't like that.
Interesting. Tool use under extreme stress. Very promising data.
on_catch: There you are, Subject 7. The deep ones were right — you do have remarkable survival instincts. Now, let's begin the real experiment.
Subject 7, captured. Commencing pressure adaptation protocol. This will be... uncomfortable.

effects.text: Tanaka slams the dive locker shut and reattaches a new padlock. "Equipment is off-limits, Subject 7. The experiment requires controlled conditions."
Tanaka notices the open deck grate. She kicks it back into place. "Stay out of the bilge channels. The specimens sometimes travel through the drainage system."
Tanaka peers at the open ventilation shaft. "Resourceful. But the shaft is too narrow for you. And sound carries both ways."

special_behaviors.description: Tanaka rushes to protect her specimens from the bioluminescent lure.
Tanaka is locked out by the jammed bulkhead — she can still flood the module but can't enter.

win_conditions.description: Repair the communications system, tune to the backup frequency, and send a mayday. Survive until rescue arrives by sealing hull breaches and avoiding Tanaka.
Unlock the emergency ascent pod with the override code, repair the dive helmet, secure an air supply, and launch to the surface.
Close the flood valves, redirect pipe pressure, and blow the ballast tanks to surface the entire module.

lose_conditions.description: Caught by Dr. Tanaka while not hiding.

lose_conditions.message: The hull gives way. The ocean rushes in — a wall of black water and crushing pressure. The last thing you see is the bioluminescent creatures flooding through the breach, pulsing in triumph. Dr. Tanaka's voice over the intercom, serene: 'The Mother welcomes you, Subject 7.'
lose_conditions.description: Module B suffers catastrophic structural failure.

hints.text: You're zip-tied to the chair. The ties are industrial but not indestructible. Try struggling against them.
Look around carefully. The lab bench has equipment and papers that could be useful.
That UV penlight is used for finding things invisible to the naked eye. Try it on documents...
Dive equipment often comes with multi-tools. Check the suit rack area.
The emergency panel needs a code matching the station registry number. Look for registration markings on station equipment.
The radio needs a replacement circuit board and a spliced antenna cable. The supply crate and comms station have what you need.
To surface the whole module: seal hull breaches, close flood valves with the valve key, redirect pipe pressure, then solve the ballast toggle pattern.
The ascent pod needs both electronic override AND manual lever. Enter the station registry code on the override keypad.
The specimens react to bioluminescent signals, and Tanaka is obsessed with protecting them. Combining the sample and flare could create a powerful distraction.
The flood valves need a square-socket key. Something metallic glints under the deck grate...

solution_paths.name: Call for Rescue
solution_paths.description: Repair the sabotaged communications system, find the hidden backup frequency, and call for rescue. Then survive by sealing hull breaches and evading Tanaka.

steps.action: Struggle free from zip ties (hand chair)
Search lab bench (hand) — get crew log page + UV penlight
Take multi-tool from dive suit rack
Open supply crate (hand) — get sealant tube + cable segment + learn code 0451
Combine cable segment + multi-tool — get repaired antenna cable
Go to comms closeup, use circuit board + repaired cable on radio console
Use UV penlight on logbook — learn backup frequency 156.8
Tune frequency dial to 156.8 MHz
Talk into handset — send mayday
Seal ceiling pipe crack with sealant
steps.note: Buy time for rescue to arrive

steps.action: Survive until rescue (use hiding spots, camouflage evidence)

solution_paths.name: Emergency Ascent
solution_paths.description: Unlock and launch the emergency ascent pod. Requires the override code, a sealed dive helmet, and air supply.

steps.action: Struggle free from zip ties
Take multi-tool from suit rack
Open supply crate — get sealant + cable + learn code 0451
Enter code 0451 on emergency keypad
Go to pressure control closeup
Open dive locker with multi-tool
Go to dive equipment closeup
Open toolbox — get pressure wrench + replacement visor
Take air tank + emergency flare from rack
Combine visor + sealant on dive helmet — fix visor
Read depth chart — learn pod requirements
Enter override code on override panel keypad
Pull ascent lever with helmet + air tank equipped

solution_paths.name: Surface the Module
solution_paths.description: Close flood valves, redirect pipe pressure, and blow all ballast tanks to surface the entire station module. The loudest, most dramatic escape.

steps.action: Struggle free from zip ties
Take multi-tool from suit rack
Open supply crate — get sealant + cable + learn code 0451
Seal ceiling pipe crack with sealant
Remove deck grate with multi-tool — get valve key
Enter code 0451 on emergency keypad
Go to pressure control closeup
Use valve key on flood valve array — close all valves
Use valve key on ceiling pipes — redirect pressure
Activate ballast panel (now unlocked)
Solve ballast toggle puzzle (lights-out mechanic)
Module surfaces!
